chunks: And from him, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Musa ibn 'Imran, from 'Abdullah al-Hajjal, from Safwan al-Jammal, who said:

I heard Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) used to go out in the presence of a group of people from his companions every Thursday evening to the Baqi' of the Medinans, and he would say three times: 'Peace be upon you, O people of the dwellings,' and three times: 'May Allah have mercy on you.' Then he would turn to his companions and say, 'These are better than you.' So they would say, 'O Messenger of Allah, why? They believed and we believed, and they fought and we fought.' He would say, 'Indeed, these believed and did not mix their faith with oppression, and they passed away upon that [and I am a witness to that for them. However, you will remain after me and I do not know what you will instigate after me.'

key_terms.أَهْلَ الدِّيَارِ: People of the dwellings (referring to the deceased in their graves)
key_terms.مَضَوْا عَلَى ذَلِكَ: They passed away upon that state

ai.seo_question: Why did the Prophet consider the deceased better than the living companions?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (a.s.) highlights the Prophet’s (s.a.w.) Thursday evening visits to Baqi’ as a ritual emphasizing the spiritual superiority of the deceased, whose faith remained untainted by the 'oppression' (zulm) that would later afflict the living. This narration underscores the Shia concept of the inevitability of post-Prophetic trials (fitan) and serves as a theological basis for the merit of Ziyārah, linking the purity of the dead to the enduring uncertainty of the living community.
